extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, policymakers, and researchers interested in aviation safety and the Boeing 737 MAX crisis
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article summarizing stakeholder reactions, investigations, regulatory and corporate responses, and commentary around the Boeing 737 MAX crashes and grounding. It aggregates quotes, expert opinions, regulatory actions, and media coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of accident investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: An accident investigation is not about blame, is not only about what happened, but rather strives to identify the root causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by Christine Negroni as a counterpoint to assigning pilot blame; investigations should focus on systemic root causes and contributing factors rather than solely attributing fault to individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Airmanship / pilot competence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pilots must be capable of absolute mastery of the aircraft and the situation at all times, a concept pilots call airmanship."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captain Chesley Sullenberger emphasizes high pilot skill and training as necessary, while noting that inadequate training does not excuse fundamentally unsafe aircraft design (e.g., MCAS described as a 'death trap').

rubrics_metrics.name: Require simulator training for 737 MAX pilots
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer advocates (Flyers Rights) and others argued against the FAA's position of not requiring simulator training for 737 MAX pilots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flyers Rights asked to extend comment periods to allow expert input and demanded simulator training; calls were made for regulators to mandate differential/simulator training before return-to-service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and independent review prior to ungrounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocates sued or petitioned for access to Boeing 737 MAX records and argued for transparency and independent review before the MAX is ungrounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flyers Rights sued the FAA for refusal to allow access to Boeing records, arguing decisions should be based on independent examination of documentation rather than only manufacturer/regulator assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground aircraft when evidence indicates safety risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Former NTSB chairman Jim Hall said the FAA should ground the airplane when safety concerns warrant it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators are expected to act (including grounding) when investigations or evidence suggest systemic safety risks; this contrasts with initial FAA statements asserting no basis to ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit delegation that undermines oversight (critique of ODA expansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that Congress and FAA delegated excessive authority to industry via the Organization Delegation Authorization (ODA) program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Goglia and others warned that delegating certification/oversight to manufacturers undermines independent scrutiny and can expose oversight engineers to management pressure, producing chilling effects on safety advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to standard certification processes (do not circumvent)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Boeing has found a willing partner in the FAA, which allowed the company to circumvent standard certification processes so it could sell aircraft more quickly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hall and Goelz argued that circumventing certification procedures is unacceptable; certification must be thorough and not expedited at the expense of safety, with comparisons to prior certification controversies (e.g., 737 rudder issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board and governance responsibility for safety risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate boards and audit committees are responsible for proactively identifying safety risks and exercising oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance experts (Nell Minow, Glass Lewis) criticized Boeing's board for lacking relevant expertise and failing to act after the first crash; shareholder advisory recommendations emphasized voting against directors who failed in oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational culture must empower employees and encourage reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing needs a full organizational culture change to empower employees to raise concerns without fear and to root out arrogance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (Amy Edmondson, Neal Hartman, Rosabeth Moss Kanter) state that culture changes are necessary: employees must feel safe to report problems, and leadership must listen to regulators, unions, suppliers and employees to restore trust and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and strengthen engineering oversight and culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing should retain an engineering culture and strong engineering management; deviation from that standard was criticized as a cause of problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts (Richard Aboulafia) argued Boeing deviated from engineering management principles; calls for bolstered engineering oversight and structural changes to restore technical rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid outsourcing critical software work without adequate quality controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns raised that key software work (MCAS) was outsourced to low-cost contractors, potentially jeopardizing safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting (Bloomberg, others) suggested cost-cutting and outsourcing correlated with reduced testing and oversight; firms should ensure high-quality, well-tested software development for flight-critical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include new features/systems details in flight operations manuals and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators and senators questioned why flight operations manuals and training did not include details of new features/systems like MCAS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kyrsten Sinema and others asked for more detailed documentation and training materials so pilots understand new systems and can respond appropriately in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: National regulators should make independent recertification decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for regulators (e.g., Transport Canada) not to rely solely on FAA decisions when deciding on ungrounding or recertification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ralph Nader and others urged national regulators to perform independent assessments rather than deferring to the FAA, emphasizing sovereign responsibility for passenger safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective crisis communications and stakeholder engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing's communications with Congress, regulators, customers, victims' families and the public were criticized as poor crisis management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts (Richard Aboulafia, others) noted that transparent, timely, and credible communication is crucial to restoring trust; mishandled messaging intensifies reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough testing and verification of software fixes before return-to-service
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing reported numerous test flights and software fixes (e.g., 96 or 500 test flights) as part of the response to MCAS issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate, well-documented flight testing and independent verification of software updates are necessary prerequisites for recertification and restoring confidence among regulators and airlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure access to internal documents and protect whistleblower disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Release of internal emails and documents and whistleblower complaints highlighted the need for regulators/investigators to access internal communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency of internal communications and protection for whistleblowers are important for uncovering systemic problems and preventing chilling effects from management discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory independence, adequate resourcing, and protection from industry pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that the FAA was understaffed, underfunded, and too close to industry, which damaged its ability to regulate effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers argued regulators need sufficient staff, funding and independence from industry influence to carry out rigorous certification and oversight duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect heightened scrutiny for future certifications
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is going to be the most scrutinized certification in history."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts predicted that recertification and future certification processes for the MAX and similar projects would be subject to intense review by regulators, media, and stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design safety: evaluate structural design and engine-airframe compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that the 737 MAX had structural design issues — e.g., engines too large for the traditional fuselage — leading some (Ralph Nader) to call it a structural design defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aircraft design decisions must consider structural compatibility and the aerodynamic implications of larger engines or other major changes to legacy designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect oversight engineers from management pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing or disciplining engineers who press for more testing can produce a chilling effect and 'negate the whole system.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Goglia and others argued that protecting the independence and job security of oversight engineers is essential to maintain rigorous safety testing and reporting within manufacturers and regulatory bodies.
